content.title: About
content.content: Black-eyed peas (Vigna unguiculata) are dried beans also known as “cowpeas” or “southern peas.” Originating from Africa, they are now cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. The beans have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor and a firm yet tender texture when cooked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black-eyed peas belong to the legume family and are closely related to beans and chickpeas.
They are a staple of Southern U.S. cuisine, famously used in dishes like Hoppin’ John and succotash.
In many African cultures the peas are considered a symbol of good luck and are served at celebrations.
Dry peas can be stored for 2–3 years when kept in proper conditions.
Because of their high starch content, cooked peas become creamy and thick.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked black-eyed peas provides about 13 g of protein, making them a valuable meat alternative for vegetarians.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestive health and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients are essential for blood formation and can help prevent anemia, especially in women of childbearing age.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The peas raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for diabetes management and weight control.

items.title: High in antioxidants
items.content: Phytochemicals such as flavonoids help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to legumes, including black-eyed peas.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Dry beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and sprouting can mitigate this.

items.title: Potential toxins
items.content: Raw beans contain lectins that can be toxic; they must be fully cooked before consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak dry black-eyed peas for 6‑8 hours, then simmer for 45‑60 minutes until tender. They are used in soups, stews, salads, mashed as a dip, or as a filling for vegetables. They also work well in veggie burgers or the classic Southern side dish “rice and peas.”

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry black-eyed peas in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage (over a year), keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold growth and flavor loss.
